title: The reference that goes stale
promptHtml:
running_max walks a vector, remembering a reference to the largest element seen so far, and appends a running total to the same vector as it goes. Because it appends, the vector reallocates — and the remembered reference is left pointing into a freed block.

Fix it so the function is correct for any input size. Do not change what it returns or stop it appending; the appends are the point.

The checks run under AddressSanitizer, so reading through a stale reference fails rather than silently returning a plausible number.
hints:
int& best = values[0]; names a location inside the vector’s buffer. push_back may move that buffer.

An index survives reallocation; a reference does not. Track the best value or its index instead of a reference to it.

The simplest fix is one word: make best an int rather than an int&.

Be careful to keep the behaviour identical — best is read when computing the appended value, so it must be updated before the push_back as it was before.
solutionNotesHtml:
The fix is a single character, which is the uncomfortable part: nothing about the broken version looks wrong. int& reads as an efficiency-minded choice, and for a container that is not being modified it would be a fine one.

Note that the small cases can pass even when broken. With three elements the vector may have spare capacity and never reallocate, so the reference stays valid by luck. The 500-element case is there to force several reallocations — which is exactly how this bug behaves in production: fine in tests, wrong on real data.

The general rule is in the chapter: do not hold a pointer, reference, or iterator across an operation that can change the container’s size. When you need to remember a position, remember an index.
